rows.notes: The cited document is a narrative review with an embedded global meta-analysis (Section 4, Figure 5) pooling 1164 comparisons from 117 publications; it reports no own field, survey or model data. Reviews and meta-analyses are 'no' for Q1. The meta-analysis does report that drip at <100% of the water of flood/furrow gives higher yield and improved WP/IWP with 95% CIs, but this is a synthesis of other studies, not primary evidence.

Review/meta-analysis, not a primary study. The pooled result (Section 4.1, Figure 5) that drip at <100% water gives significantly higher yields than flooding (95% CI 6.12<U+2013>7.55%) and furrow (6.74<U+2013>7.93%) but no significant difference versus border or micro-sprinkler is a synthesis of 117 publications, not the authors' own experiment.

Review/meta-analysis, not a primary study. The document does not present any own result on risk management; the statement that drip 'has been proven to save water and maintain crop yields' under water shortage (Section 4.1) is a synthesis of pooled literature.

Review/meta-analysis, not a primary study. The pooled meta-analysis actually reports no significant yield difference between drip and border or micro-sprinkler irrigation when drip water is <100% of the control (Section 4.1, Figure 5), which loosely relates to the claim, but it is a synthesis of other studies and the review itself does not attribute this to water not being the limiting factor.

Review, not a primary study. Emitter clogging is discussed descriptively in Sections 2 and 8.2 (narrow channels susceptible to blockage, poor maintenance leading to system failure) and salt accumulation in wide rows/inter-membrane zones is reported from Wu et al. [111] and Ma et al. [112] in Section 7; none of this is the authors' own data, and no own result links these to reduced crop production.

Review, not a primary study. Section 7 summarises other work (e.g., [106], [111], [112]) on salt accumulation at the edges of wetted zones and in wide rows under mulched drip; no own data on soil health harm.

Review, not a primary study. The description of drip delivering water and fertilizer to the root zone and reducing evaporation/seepage (Introduction, Section 2) is narrative, citing other work [4<U+2013>8]; no own measurement of evaporation or water conservation.

notes: The cited document is a narrative review of drip irrigation in China that includes a global meta-analysis of 117 publications (Figure 5, yield/WP/IWP with 95% CIs) and a bibliometric analysis (Web of Science/CNKI counts). It reports no primary field, survey or validated model data, so all rows are Q1 = 'no' per the instructions on reviews and meta-analyses. Text appears complete.
